title: Garuda
wiki_lead:
Garuda (Sanskrit: गरुड, romanized: Garuḍa; Pali: गरुळ, romanized: Garuḷa) is a Hindu deity who is primarily depicted as the mount (vahana) of the Hindu god Vishnu. Garuda is mentioned in the Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain faiths. He is also the half-brother of the Devas, Gandharvas, Daityas, Danavas, Nāgas, Vanaras and Yakshas. He is the son of the sage Kashyapa and Vinata. He is the younger brother of Aruna, the charioteer of the Sun. Garuda is mentioned in several other texts such as the Puranas and the Vedas.
Garuda is described as the king of the birds and a kite-like figure. He is shown either in a zoomorphic form (a giant bird with partially open wings) or an anthropomorphic form (a man with wings and some bird-like features). Garuda is generally portrayed as a protector with the power to swiftly travel anywhere, ever vigilant and an enemy of every serpent. He is also known as Tarkshya and Vainateya.
Garuda is a part of the state insignia of India, Indonesia and Thailand. Both Indonesia and Thailand have Garuda as their coat of arms, and the Indian Army uses the Garuda on its Guards Brigade Regimental Insignia. The Indian Air Force named their special operations unit after him as the Garud Commando Force.
The name Garuda is often associated with the Greater adjutant stork (Leptoptilos dubius).

Hinduism

In Hinduism, Garuda is a divine eagle-like sun bird and the king of birds. A Garutman is mentioned in the Rigveda who is described as celestial deva with wings. The Shatapatha Brahmana embedded inside the Yajurveda text mentions Garuda as the personification of courage. In the Mahabharata, Garutman is stated to be same as Garuda, then described as the one who is fast, who can shapeshift into any form and enter anywhere. He is a powerful creature in the epics, whose wing flapping can stop the spinning of heaven, earth and hell. He is described to be the vehicle mount of the Hindu god Vishnu, and typically they are shown together. He is the younger brother of Aruna, who is a charioteer of the sun god, Surya.
According to George Williams, Garuda has roots in the verb gri, or speak. He is a metaphor in the Vedic literature for rik (rhythms), saman (sounds), yajna (sacrifices), and the atman (Self, deepest level of consciousness). Williams states that in the Puranas, Garuda becomes a literal embodiment of the idea, and the Self who attached to and inseparable from the Supreme Self (Vishnu). Though Garuda is an essential part of the Vaishnavism, he also features prominently in Shaivism, Shaiva texts such as the Garuda Tantra and Kirana Tantra, and Shiva temples as a bird and as a metaphor of atman.


Iconography

The Hindu texts on Garuda iconography vary in their details. If in the bird form, he is eagle-like, typically with the wings slightly open as if ready and willing to fly wherever he needs to. grok_lead: Garuda is a mythical bird-like creature revered in Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain traditions, most prominently known as the divine mount (vahana) of the god Vishnu in Hinduism, where it symbolizes immense power, speed, and loyalty. Depicted as a massive eagle-headed humanoid with golden wings spanning vast distances, a curved beak, and often serpents as ornaments representing its enmity with the naga (serpent) race, Garuda embodies the bridge between the earthly and divine realms. In Buddhist iconography, it serves as a protector deity against poisons and obstacles, particularly those inflicted by nagas, and is associated with figures like Vajrapani. Within Jainism, Garuda functions as a yaksha (guardian spirit) attendant to the tirthankara Shantinatha, highlighting themes of support and swift divine intervention. Originating from ancient Indian mythology, Garuda is the son of the sage Kashyapa and the bird-woman Vinata, hatched from an egg after a prolonged gestation of five hundred years, emerging with a radiant, blazing form that shook the universe. A central myth recounts Garuda's heroic quest to free his mother from enslavement by his stepmother Kadru's naga children; to achieve this, he battled the gods to steal the pot of amrita (immortal nectar) from heaven, ultimately securing his freedom through a pact with Vishnu, by which Garuda agreed to serve eternally as his mount. This tale, detailed in epics like the Mahabharata and Ramayana, establishes Garuda as the king of birds and a devoted servant, often portrayed carrying Vishnu or Lakshmi on his back in temple sculptures and texts such as the Garuda Purana, a Vaishnava scripture narrated by Garuda himself on topics like death, reincarnation, and dharma. Beyond mythology, Garuda's iconography influences art, architecture, and symbolism across Asia, appearing in temple reliefs, dances, and national emblemsâsuch as Indonesia's coat of arms âwhere it represents sovereignty and freedom derived from its liberating myths. In esoteric traditions, including Tantric Buddhism, Garuda rituals invoke protection from physical and spiritual afflictions, underscoring its enduring role as a emblem of courage and transcendence.
